Newborn plains viscachas emerge from the womb weighing approximately 200 grams [Wwb = approximately 200 grams], a substantial birth mass for a precocial rodent. This relatively large neonatal size reflects an extended gestation period, which under the species' typical core body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C] lasts for 154 days [tg = 154 days]. Such a prolonged uterine development, unusual among caviomorph rodents, permits advanced maturation of the central nervous system and musculoskeletal apparatus, enabling pups to follow their mother and consume solid vegetation within hours of parturition. The elevated birth mass is also tightly linked to the species' life-history strategy; females invest heavily in a small number of well-developed offspring rather than producing a larger litter of altricial young. This gestational investment, measured under stable thermal conditions, underpins the rapid postnatal growth phase that characterizes the early weeks of life in this species.

Lactation in the plains viscacha is relatively brief compared to other rodents of similar body size, with the weaning process culminating at approximately 54 days after birth [tx = approximately 54 days after birth] when measured at the species' typical body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C]. By this point, the weanling has attained a wet weight of 652.2 grams [Wwx = 652.2 grams], representing more than a threefold increase from its birth mass. This impressive growth trajectory is fueled by the mother's exceptionally rich milk, which contains high lipid and protein concentrations suited to supporting rapid somatic development. The shift from a milk-based diet to one dominated by tough, fibrous grasses marks a critical nutritional transition, and weanlings must develop a functional cecal fermentation system to extract sufficient energy from their new forage. Mortality during this periveaning period can be substantial, particularly when environmental conditions delay the emergence of high-quality green vegetation.

Reproductive output in female plains viscachas is characterized by moderate litter sizes and frequent breeding opportunities. A typical female produces 2 pups per litter [N_R_i = 2 pups per litter] under favorable conditions, a figure that aligns with the species' K-selected strategy within the context of large-bodied rodents. When the ambient or body temperature is maintained at 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output approaches a rate of approximately 1.8 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.8 litters per year], yielding a total of roughly 3.6 pups annually. This frequency is enabled by a postpartum estrus that allows females to conceive again shortly after giving birth. Such a pattern of continuous reproduction, unimpeded by strict seasonal constraints in many parts of the viscacha's range, permits rapid population turnover and recolonization of disturbed habitats, though it comes at a substantial energetic cost to the lactating female.

Sexual maturation in the plains viscacha is strongly dimorphic, with a pronounced difference between the sexes in the timing of puberty. Females attain reproductive maturity relatively early, reaching puberty at 258 days after birth [tp = 258 days after birth] at a core body temperature of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], a developmental schedule that permits them to begin breeding within their first year of life. Males, in contrast, experience a considerably delayed sexual maturation, reaching puberty at 456 days after birth [tp = 456 days after birth], but crucially at a scrotal temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C], which is elevated compared to the core body temperature and reflects the specific thermoregulatory requirements of spermatogenesis. This delay in male maturity is hypothesized to result from intense intrasexual competition for access to females; larger, older males who have had more time to develop robust body condition and fighting ability are disproportionately successful in defending harems and siring offspring.

Longevity records for the plains viscacha indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 10.8 years [am = approximately 10.8 years] under the core body temperature regime of 36.8 °C [T = 36.8 °C], a figure that places this species among the longer-lived members of the Caviidae. This extended lifespan is consistent with the relatively slow pace of life history exhibited by this large, herbivorous rodent, which invests heavily in each reproductive event and experiences low natural adult mortality in the absence of its primary predators. The ultimate adult wet weight attained by a fully grown individual can reach 6000 grams [Wwi = 6000 grams], making the plains viscacha one of the heaviest extant rodents. Such a large body size confers advantages in predator defense and thermal buffering against the cold, arid winters of the Argentine Pampas, but also imposes substantial absolute energetic demands that must be met through a high daily intake of fibrous, low-quality forage.
